attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, said in his own voice.

semantics.note: The wording matches: hallucination is inherent ('feature, not a bug') because the models know nothing and guess by calculation. 'Know anything' is undefined, and the passage reads partly as rhetoric.

contract.note: The contract rightly sets no single test. Whether the claim is true depends on what 'knowing' means, and the speaker never says.

evidence.note: ROME study shows models store factual associations. That cuts against a 'no stored information' reading but does not settle knowledge in the speaker's sense.
Kalai & Vempala give conditional lower bounds and say hallucination is not inevitable. Relevant to the inherence reading, but the result is not tied to the speaker's undefined terms.

reviews.rationale: This is a loose causal claim built on the undefined idea of models 'knowing anything', mixed with the rhetorical 'feature, not a bug'. The evidence bears on some readings but cannot score the claim without choosing a meaning the speaker never gave.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, said in his own voice.

semantics.note: The claim is about how LLMs work: they do not learn, they copy others' likely-correct answers. The 'plagiarize' part is partly an ethical label, and the contract rightly leaves it unscored.

contract.note: 'That's not how they work' is a claim about mechanism. Reading 'learning' as fitting statistical structure that lets a model generalise, rather than human understanding, is an ordinary, fair reading. The ethical framing is set aside.

evidence.note: GPT-4 report says the model is pre-trained to predict the next token. That is a company describing its own training method, not an independent finding.
Controlled tests on problems built to be new show solutions beyond repeating stored answers. That is evidence of learned structure.
Shows verbatim memorisation in some cases. This can coexist with learning and does not show copying is the only mechanism.
Narrows e2's reasoning claims but does not show the outputs are copied answers.

reviews.rationale: Read plainly, the claim is that models only copy others' answers and do not learn. Technical records show training on next-token prediction, and independent tests on new problems show abilities beyond verbatim copying. Memorisation evidence limits but does not save the claim. The 'plagiarism' ethics are not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, said in his own voice.

semantics.note: A firm 'they'll' forecast that depends on desperation over data scarcity, which the surrounding text supplies. No company, model or deadline is named.

contract.note: Requiring a real company model to collapse from scarcity-driven ingestion is a fair reading of 'destroys'. The contract also rightly says the absence of collapse so far proves nothing.

evidence.note: Lab result: collapse when data is replaced, none when it is accumulated. Lab work does not meet the early-resolution rule and does not show the antecedent.
Microsoft's own account of heavy, deliberate synthetic-data use in Phi-4. It shows neither scarcity-driven desperation nor collapse.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated and no dated, documented collapse of a company model meets the early-resolution rule. Whether the antecedent (scarcity-driven desperation) has occurred is unknown. The evidence available by the cutoff cannot score the forecast.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He cites the study as support, but the causal claim is his.

semantics.note: Says lax moderation led to a flood of AI content on Facebook. The causal link and the scope are kept.

contract.note: Reading 'flooded' as substantial distribution, not a majority of content, is fair. Requiring that moderation materially enabled it follows directly from 'led to'.

evidence.note: Researchers document 100+ high-volume AI-image pages that may be boosted by recommendations. This supports the 'flood' part only; moderation is not shown as the cause.
The peer-reviewed version says its page sample is not representative of Facebook overall and does not test moderation effects.
Meta's description of its own moderation measures. It does not show they work, and it is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows AI content spreading widely across many Facebook pages before the post, which partly supports the 'flood'. Nothing separates weak moderation from recommendation algorithms or ad-money incentives, so the 'led to' link is neither shown nor refuted.
